cards.explanation: The answer is False. God tells Moses that a priest is not to defile himself for a dead person among his people. Then verse 2 starts a short list of exceptions. So the opening rule is the starting point, friends, and the exceptions are part of the picture too.

The answer is his unmarried sister. Verse 3 names his unmarried sister who is near to him, since she has no husband. She joins his mother, father, son, daughter and brother on the list. The text gives that reason, so I'll stick with it.

The answer is False. Verse 4 says he is not to defile himself for those related to him by marriage, and so profane himself. The family exceptions just before it were his mother, father, son, daughter, brother and unmarried sister. Relatives by marriage aren't on that list.

The answer is making cuts in their bodies. Verse 5 says priests must not make bald spots on their heads, shave off the edges of their beards, or make cuts in their bodies. That's three things, friends, and cuts are the third. I read all three and checked my own mustache twice, just to be safe.

The answer is that they present the LORD's food offerings. Verse 6 says they present to the LORD the food offerings, the food of their God, and that's why "…they must be holy." Think about handing someone a cookie box for a big celebration. I'm wiping the chocolate off my mustache first. Handling something that belongs to God is a much bigger deal than that.

The answer is True. In verse 8 God says the priest shall be holy to the people, "…because I the LORD am holy…" He adds that He is the One who sets them apart. The holiness starts with who God is, friends, and it all flows from there.

The answer is False. Verse 11 says the highest priest must not go near any dead body, and he must not defile himself, even for his father or mother. For regular priests, mother and father were on the exception list in verse 2. His rule is stricter, and I think that's a hard one.

The answer is that the anointing oil of his God is on him. Verse 12 says the consecration of the anointing oil of his God is on him, and verse 10 says that oil was poured on his head. Flour on my hat only means I've been working. This oil means God set him apart, friends. That's the reason the text gives for not leaving or desecrating the sanctuary.

The answer is False. Verse 14 says he is not to marry a widow, a divorced woman, or one defiled by prostitution. He is to marry a virgin from his own people. That's a longer list than the one for regular priests in verse 7.

The answer is so he does not defile his offspring. Verse 15 says he marries a virgin from his own people so that he does not defile his offspring among his people. Then God says, "…for I am the LORD who sanctifies him." The reason comes straight from the text, friends.

The answer is False. Verse 17 says that for the generations to come, none of Aaron's descendants who has a physical defect may approach to offer the food of his God. It's a rule for the long haul. I think it's a lot to take in, friends, and that's what the text says.

The answer is True. Verse 22 says he may eat the most holy food of his God as well as the holy food. A descendant of Aaron with a defect can't offer it, but he's still allowed to eat it. He's still one of Aaron's family, and that's the part of this passage I'd hate for anyone to miss.

The answer is so he won't desecrate God's sanctuaries. Verse 23 says that because of his defect, he must not go near the veil or approach the altar, so as not to desecrate My sanctuaries. Notice who is speaking there, friends: God Himself, calling them His. Then He adds, "For I am the LORD who sanctifies them." That's like a friend handing you the keys to their house and saying, "Hey, treat it right."

The answer is Aaron and his sons and all the Israelites. Verse 24 says Moses told this to Aaron and his sons and to all the Israelites. So it wasn't kept between the priests, friends. Everybody heard it.
